traveler: Diogenes of Sinope (Diogenes the Cynic, ho Kyon, 'the Dog')
title: Deface the Currency: the Banker's Son, the Jar, and the Lamp at Midday
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Sinope: the Coin and the Oracle

stops.name: Sinope, birth in the house of Hicesias
stops.date_confidence: traditional; modern scholars place the birth anywhere between c. 412 and c. 404 BCE
stops.campa: Sinope stands on an isthmus of the Black Sea coast, a Milesian colony grown rich on tunny, timber, and the grain traffic between Paphlagonia and the Aegean. Into a banker's house there a son is born to Hicesias, who handles other men's silver for a living and holds some office about the city's coinage. The boy is given letters, verse, wrestling, and horsemanship, the education of a family with standing. Diogenes Laertius reports the father's name and the father's trade and almost nothing else; the years between the birth and the scandal are blank.
suggested_refs: The isthmus and double harbor of ancient Sinope, Milesian colony of the Black Sea coast
sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Eminent Philosophers 6.20
Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Diogenes of Sinope'

stops.name: Sinope, the trapeza and the mint
stops.date_confidence: the pin follows the traditional bracket for the scandal, c. 362 BCE, so that the sequence holds; the numismatic evidence dates the debased Sinopean silver to c. 350-340 BCE, later issues carrying the magistrate name Hikesio, a decade or more after the traditional exile, and the disagreement is left standing rather than resolved
stops.campa: Sinope strikes silver drachms with an eagle standing on a dolphin, and for a stretch of years the issues come out adulterated or driven through with a punch. Later dies carry the magistrate's name, Hikesio. Diogenes Laertius sets down three versions of what happened and chooses none: that Hicesias alone debased the coin and died in prison for it, that father and son did it together, that the son did it and the father paid. In a treatise of his own called the Pordalos, now lost, Diogenes is said to have admitted the guilt was his.
stops.quote: Diocles relates that he went into exile because his father was entrusted with the money of the state and adulterated the coinage.
suggested_refs: Surviving Sinopean silver drachms of the eagle-on-dolphin type, including the countermarked and debased issues of c. 350-340 BCE
sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives 6.20-21, citing Diocles and Eubulides
Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Diogenes of Sinope', citing numismatic studies

stops.name: Delphi, the answer of the god
stops.date_confidence: undated in the sources; Diogenes Laertius sends him to Delphi or else to Delos, the birthplace of Apollo, and does not decide between them
stops.campa: He climbs the terrace under the Phaedriades and puts his question to the god. The answer comes back: parakharattein to politikon nomisma, change the political currency. Nomisma in Greek is coin and custom at once, the stamped metal and the stamped habit, and the qualifier the oracle adds does nothing to separate them. Diogenes Laertius says he took the word in its narrow sense first and understood the wider one only afterward. The manuscripts also send him to Delos instead, and the record does not settle which shrine he stood in.
suggested_refs: The temple terrace of Apollo at Delphi; the alternative Apolline shrine on Delos named in the same passage
sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives 6.20-21 (Greek: eis Delphous e eis Delon ten Apollonos patrida)

stops.name: Sinope, the harbor and the leaving
stops.date_confidence: the departure is undated; the traditional bracket of c. 362-355 BCE is stated more precisely than the evidence allows, and the numismatic date for the debased coinage is later still
stops.campa: He goes down to the harbor and out of the city, and no source can say under what compulsion. Some have him banished by decree, some fleeing a prosecution, some walking out of his own accord once the thing broke. Diogenes Laertius reports the argument without ending it. What the Cynics after him make of the episode is single-minded: the man who defaced the currency of Sinope becomes the man who defaces the currency of custom, and a criminal charge is rewritten into a founding act. He is later reported saying that losing the money was what drove him to philosophy.
suggested_refs: The Cynic reading of parakharattein to nomisma, from Diogenes Laertius through Dio Chrysostom's eighth oration
sources: Wikipedia, 'Diogenes' (on the uncertainty of the departure date)

segments.name: Athens: the Jar and the Lamp

stops.name: Piraeus, the landfall
stops.date_confidence: inferred; no ancient source narrates the crossing, and modern scholars place the Athenian arrival anywhere between the 360s and the mid-340s BCE
stops.campa: Nobody writes the crossing down. He comes ashore at the port of Athens owning nothing worth an inventory, and the record picks him up again only inside the walls, in anecdotes. The harbor he lands in runs on exactly the thing that ruined him: grain factors, ships' agents, money-changers at their tables testing coin against a touchstone, the whole traffic of stamped metal moving through one basin. He will live in the city above it as a resident foreigner, with no deme and no standing at law. Five miles of road bring him up from the water.
suggested_refs: The Kantharos basin of the Piraeus, commercial harbor of fourth-century Athens
sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives 6.21-22 (arrival at Athens; the route is inferred)

stops.name: Athens, Cynosarges: Antisthenes and the stick
stops.date_confidence: tradition, and strained: Antisthenes is reported dead by c. 366 BCE, before most datings of Diogenes' arrival, and no source locates the meeting at Cynosarges, which is simply where Antisthenes taught
stops.campa: Antisthenes, the old pupil of Socrates, teaches at the gymnasium outside the walls set aside for men of foreign or mixed blood, and he takes no new students. From him come the doubled cloak, the wallet, the staff, and the position that virtue is trained rather than argued. When Diogenes attaches himself anyway, Antisthenes lifts his stick and drives him off. Diogenes puts his head down under the blows and tells him to strike, since no stick is hard enough to keep him away while there is anything worth hearing.
suggested_refs: The gymnasium of Cynosarges outside the Diomeian gate, where Antisthenes taught the nothoi
sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives 6.21 (the stick), 6.13 (Antisthenes at Cynosarges)
Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Diogenes of Sinope' (doubting the master-pupil relation)

stops.name: Athens, the mouse
stops.date_confidence: traditional; Diogenes Laertius gives no place for the scene and sets it before he takes up the jar, so the Agora pin is a placeholder
stops.campa: He watches a mouse running about the floor, looking for nothing in particular, keeping no house, wanting no bedding, afraid of no dark, with no appetite for anything a mouse cannot reach. Diogenes Laertius says this is what settled his manner of life. Whatever can be taken away without ending the life was never needed in the first place. So he folds his cloak double to sleep in it, takes a wallet to carry his food, later carries a staff, and calls the outfit sufficient.
suggested_refs: The Cynic kit: tribon doubled for sleeping, pera, and staff, first assembled in Athens

stops.name: Athens, the pithos at the Metroon
stops.date_confidence: traditional
stops.campa: A pithos is a storage jar for grain or oil, man-height, fired clay, too heavy to shift once full and worthless once cracked. He takes one to live in, in the precinct of the Mother of the Gods, where the city keeps its archive of laws and decrees. Latin translation later turns it into a tub and English keeps the tub, but the thing is a jar. So he sleeps against the wall of the building that holds every statute Athens has passed, inside a container the city built for surplus. For the fact Diogenes Laertius cites the man's own letters.
stops.quote: He took for his abode the tub in the Metroon, as he himself explains in his letters.
suggested_refs: The Metroon in the Athenian Agora, sanctuary of the Mother of the Gods and repository of the state archive

stops.name: Athens, the jar broken and replaced
stops.date_confidence: traditional
stops.campa: A boy breaks the jar. The Athenians give him another one. The city doing the giving has heard him call its assemblies foolish and its magistrates worse, and it replaces his house anyway. He holds nothing the law counts as property and nothing the law counts as standing, and the demos supplies him a jar. Diogenes Laertius reports the replacement in a line and does not say who proposed it, what it cost the city, or whether it was one jar or a succession of them.
suggested_refs: The replacement of the philosopher's jar at public expense, reported among the Athenian anecdotes

stops.name: Athens, the lamp at midday
stops.date_confidence: traditional
stops.campa: At midday, with the sun standing over the Agora and every stall in full light, he walks through the crowd carrying a lit lamp. Asked what he is doing, he says he is looking for a man. Later ages make it an honest man; the Greek says only anthropon zeto, and the ones he passes, buying fish, arguing prices, voting, are apparently not it. The instrument is a lychnos, a clay oil lamp, and it burns for nothing in broad daylight. Diogenes Laertius gives the scene in one sentence and offers no gloss on it.
stops.quote: He lit a lamp in broad daylight and said, as he went about, 'I am looking for a man.'
suggested_refs: Fourth-century Attic clay lychnoi of the type carried in the anecdote

stops.name: Athens, the works of Demeter and of Aphrodite
stops.date_confidence: traditional
stops.campa: He eats in the marketplace, which Athenians hold to be indecent, and argues that if breakfast is not shameful in itself then it is not shameful anywhere. He takes the same reasoning further and masturbates in the open square, in front of whoever is standing there. The disgust of the crowd is the point of the demonstration: nature did not put that disgust there, the city did. His own remark on it is a complaint about the unfairness of the appetites, that hunger cannot be got rid of as easily, by rubbing the belly.
stops.quote: It was his habit to do everything in public, the works of Demeter and of Aphrodite alike.
suggested_refs: The Cynic doctrine of anaideia, shamelessness, argued from the indifference of natural acts

stops.name: Athens, begging from the statues
stops.date_confidence: traditional
stops.campa: He stands in front of a bronze figure on its base, puts out his hand, and asks it for money. People ask why. He says he is practicing being refused. A statue cannot give and cannot be shamed into giving, which is the whole of its use to him: the refusal comes back clean every time, and the practice can be repeated all day. Diogenes Laertius files the habit with the rest of the training, the rolling in hot sand through the summer and the embracing of snow-covered statues through the winter.
suggested_refs: The Cynic askesis of deliberate hardship, drilled in the Athenian Agora

stops.name: Athens, Manes runs away
stops.date_confidence: traditional
stops.campa: He owns one slave, a man called Manes, and Manes runs off. Friends tell him to go after him. He answers that it would be ridiculous if Manes can get on without Diogenes while Diogenes cannot get on without Manes, and lets him go. It is the one piece of ordinary property the record still allows him at this date, and the loss is entered on the credit side of his own ledger. Diogenes Laertius gives the runaway three lines and no sequel. Nothing further is heard of Manes.
suggested_refs: The runaway Manes, the last item of household property attributed to Diogenes

stops.name: Athens, taking the name of the Dog
stops.date_confidence: traditional
stops.campa: Kyon, dog: the word is thrown at him for eating in the street, sleeping anywhere, coupling in public, and biting people who deserve it. He takes the name and keeps it, and the school that follows him is called kynikos after it. Asked why he is called a dog, he says he fawns on those who give him something, barks at those who give nothing, and sets his teeth in scoundrels. In a Greek city the dog lives at the edge of the household, fed at the door and tolerated and never quite let inside.
suggested_refs: The epithet kyon and the derivation of kynikos, Cynic, from it

stops.name: Athens, citizen of the world
stops.date_confidence: traditional
stops.campa: Asked where he comes from, he answers that he is a citizen of the world. Every man in the marketplace who hears it belongs to a deme, a phratry, a tribe, and a city with the power to expel him; the resident foreigners standing there belong in the same way to some other such city instead. He claims none of it, having been thrown out of the one city that could have claimed him. The Greek word is kosmopolites. This single line of Diogenes Laertius is the earliest surviving use of it in that sense, and the biographer gives it no setting beyond the question and the answer.
suggested_refs: Kosmopolites: the earliest attested use of the word in its cosmopolitan sense

stops.name: Athens, Plato's house: the trampled carpets
stops.date_confidence: traditional; Diogenes Laertius sets the scene at Plato's own house, entertaining friends of Dionysius, and the site of that house is unknown, so the Academy coordinates stand in
stops.campa: Plato is entertaining friends of Dionysius of Syracuse and has had fine carpets laid down for them. Diogenes walks in across the carpets, treading them flat, and says that so he tramples on the pride of Plato. Plato answers that he does it with pride of his own. The two of them keep this going for years, and Diogenes Laertius sets down both men's lines without taking a side. Diogenes calls the lecturing a waste of breath and the Forms a fiction. Plato, asked what sort of man this is, calls him a Socrates gone mad.
suggested_refs: The reported exchanges between Diogenes and Plato collected in Diogenes Laertius, Book 6
sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives 6.26 (the carpets, at Plato's house), 6.54 ('a Socrates gone mad')

stops.name: Athens, the Academy: the plucked fowl
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the anecdote is undated and its setting in the lecture room is the biographer's framing
stops.campa: In the grove of Akademos, along the road out through the Dipylon gate, the school is at work on definitions. Man, they settle, is a two-footed animal without feathers, and the definition is applauded. Diogenes plucks a chicken, carries it in, and puts it down live among them with the words, here is Plato's man. Diogenes Laertius ends the story with the school amending its definition to read: having broad nails. Whether the bird was returned to anybody, or what the pupils did next, is not recorded.
suggested_refs: The grove of Akademos outside the Dipylon gate, seat of Plato's school

segments.name: The Festivals and the Marching Armies

stops.name: Corinth, the Craneum: winters at Athens, summers here
stops.date_confidence: traditional; Dio Chrysostom reports the pattern without dating it
stops.campa: Dio Chrysostom says he wintered at Athens and summered at Corinth, going up to the Isthmus for the air off two gulfs. The Craneum is a cypress grove and gymnasium outside the walls on the Kenchreai side, part exercise ground and part burial ground. He keeps his jar there and lies in the sun. Corinth is a port of shipping agents, temple prostitutes, and dealers, the richest city in Greece for a man with nothing to sell, and it holds him for the rest of his life. The ground of the Craneum has never been recovered by excavation.
suggested_refs: The Craneum outside Corinth: cypress grove, gymnasium, and burial ground, its site fixed only by ancient description

stops.name: Chaeronea, taken among the prisoners
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the anecdote is undated in Diogenes Laertius and is attached by later readers to the battle of 338 BCE
stops.campa: Philip of Macedon breaks the Greek alliance in the plain below the town, and the prisoners are brought before him. Diogenes is among them. Philip asks who he is. He answers that he is a spy upon Philip's insatiable greed. Philip laughs and lets him go. He is by now an old man walking loose across a war zone with a wallet and a stick, and the king of Macedon looks him over and finds him funny enough to let go. What he was doing at Chaeronea in the first place, no source says.
suggested_refs: The battlefield of Chaeronea, 338 BCE, and the Macedonian handling of Greek prisoners

stops.name: Corinth, the Craneum: rolling the jar
stops.date_confidence: Lucian sets the scene with Philip reported marching on Corinth, which points to 338 BCE, after Chaeronea; the month is a placeholder for that sequence
stops.campa: Word comes that Philip is marching on the city. Corinth turns out entire: men hauling stones up to the walls, sharpening weapons, patching armor, every one of them at some piece of the emergency. Diogenes has no wall to build and nobody to fight. So he takes his jar out into the Craneum and rolls it up and down, back and forth, hard, until he is out of breath. Asked what he thinks he is doing, he says that with everyone else so busy he was ashamed to be the only man idle.
suggested_refs: Lucian, How to Write History, section 3, where the jar-rolling opens a treatise on writing badly

stops.name: Isthmia, the sanctuary of Poseidon
stops.date_confidence: undated; the Isthmian material survives only through Dio Chrysostom, writing more than four centuries later with Diogenes as his speaker
stops.campa: Every second spring the Isthmus fills for the games of Poseidon, and Diogenes is remembered in that crowd, going at the victors about their pine crowns and at the bystanders about what they suppose nobility and kingship to be. The speeches themselves come down in the eighth and ninth orations of Dio Chrysostom, composed under the Roman emperors. How much of that is Cynic oral tradition carried down and how much is Dio's own rhetoric cannot be got out of the text.
suggested_refs: The sanctuary of Poseidon at Isthmia, site of the biennial games

stops.name: Olympia, the herald and Dioxippus
stops.date_confidence: the retort is undated in Diogenes Laertius; the victory of Dioxippus of Athens belongs to the 111th Olympiad, 336 BCE, and the games fell at the full moon of the Elean sacred month in late summer
stops.campa: The herald cries Dioxippus of Athens victor over men. Dioxippus is a pankratiast so large that nobody will stand up against him, and the crown is taken uncontested. Diogenes objects to the wording: Dioxippus beats slaves, he says, and it is Diogenes who beats men. The Olympic gathering is the largest audience in the Greek world, assembled in the Altis at the full moon of the sacred month, and he works it the way he works the Athenian market, one line at a time.
suggested_refs: The Altis of Olympia and the victor list of the 111th Olympiad, 336 BCE
sources: Olympic victor lists for Dioxippus of Athens (Ol. 111, akoniti pankration)

stops.name: Corinth, the Craneum: stand out of my sunlight
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the anecdote rests on Plutarch, writing more than four centuries later, with competing versions in Diogenes Laertius and no contemporary record of either man
stops.campa: The Greeks have met at the Isthmus and made Alexander their general against Persia, and everyone of consequence comes up to congratulate him. Diogenes does not. So Alexander goes to find him, and finds him lying in the sun at the Craneum, and stands over him, and offers him whatever he wants. Diogenes asks him to move a little out of the light. The king of Macedon is twenty years old and about to take Asia; the man on the ground is past seventy and owns a jar, a cloak, a wallet, and a stick.
stops.quote: When he was sunning himself in the Craneum, Alexander came and stood over him and said, 'Ask of me any boon you like.' To which he replied, 'Stand out of my light.'
suggested_refs: Diogenes' pithos at the Craneum of Corinth, where Plutarch places the meeting with Alexander

stops.name: Corinth, what Alexander said walking away
stops.date_confidence: traditional; transmitted only in the same Plutarchan passage as the meeting itself, which is one late source and not two
stops.campa: Walking off, with his companions laughing at the beggar who had turned down an empire, Alexander tells them that had he not been Alexander he would have wished to be Diogenes. The two are said to have died on the same day nine years later, one at Babylon and one at Corinth. The line survives because Plutarch wrote it down four centuries afterward. No contemporary of either man records the meeting at all, and Diogenes Laertius preserves rival versions of who said what to whom.
stops.quote: Had I not been Alexander, I should have liked to be Diogenes.
suggested_refs: The Corinth assembly of 336 BCE, at which the League named Alexander hegemon against Persia

stops.name: Aegina, the crossing that ends badly
stops.date_confidence: traditional and undated; Diogenes Laertius sources the whole episode to Menippus' Sale of Diogenes, a satire, which is reason enough to doubt it happened
stops.campa: He takes ship for Aegina, in one telling for nothing better than the pleasure of a sea bath. The Saronic gulf is crowded water, and pirates work out of its islands. The ship is taken by a crew under a captain named Scirpalus, or Harpalus depending on which manuscript is being read. This is the last point in the record at which his movements are his own. The man who has spent thirty years arguing that he owns nothing at all becomes, in open water, a thing that somebody owns.
stops.quote: On a voyage to Aegina he was captured by pirates under the command of Scirpalus, conveyed to Crete and exposed for sale.
suggested_refs: The Saronic crossing to Aegina and fourth-century piracy in the gulf

stops.name: Crete, the slave market
stops.date_confidence: traditional; no ancient source names the Cretan port and these coordinates stand in for a major harbor of the island. Diogenes Laertius 6.74 carries him to Crete, while another strand of the tradition keeps the sale at Aegina, and the two are not reconciled here
stops.campa: Crete has slave markets at several of its harbors and no source says which one this is. The pirates put him up for sale with the rest of the stock, an old man with no trade, no papers, and no city to be ransomed back to. The auctioneer asks what work he knows. He says he knows how to govern men, and tells the man to cry him for sale to anybody in the crowd who wants to buy himself a master. Then he catches sight of a Corinthian standing there, well dressed, soft-handed, spending, and points at him.
stops.quote: When the auctioneer asked in what he was proficient, he replied, 'In ruling men.'
suggested_refs: Menippus of Gadara's lost satire The Sale of Diogenes, named by Diogenes Laertius as the source of the episode
sources: Wikipedia, 'Diogenes' (noting the story is probably apocryphal)

stops.name: Crete, Xeniades pays for him
stops.date_confidence: traditional, and inseparable from the satirical source that carries the whole sale
stops.campa: Xeniades buys him, taken with the answers. Either on the spot or on the way home, Diogenes sets the terms of his own servitude: Xeniades is to do as he is told, on the ground that a doctor or a helmsman gives the orders that matter whether or not he happens to be somebody's property. He has spent his life saying that the only real slavery is to appetite and to other men's opinions, and he goes on saying it from inside the legal condition. Whether Xeniades agreed to any of this at the time, or only repeated it afterward as a good story about the man he had bought, the source does not say.
stops.quote: You must obey me, although I am a slave; for, if a physician or a steersman were in slavery, he would be obeyed.
suggested_refs: The Cynic distinction between legal servitude and slavery to appetite, argued at the point of sale

stops.name: Corinth, the household of Xeniades
stops.date_confidence: traditional
stops.campa: Brought back across the water into a rich Corinthian house, he is set over the master's two sons. He teaches them to ride, to shoot with the bow, to sling, to throw the javelin, and to hunt. He has them keep their hair cropped short, go without ornament, walk quietly in the street, eat plain food, and drink water. They wait on themselves and fetch their own bread rather than be waited on. He makes them learn passages of poetry and of his own teaching by heart, and drills them with short summaries built to hold in the memory.
suggested_refs: The Cynic curriculum given to the sons of Xeniades, the fullest account of Diogenes as a teacher

stops.name: Corinth, growing old in that house
stops.date_confidence: the sources disagree: one strand has him freed by Xeniades, another has him remain in the household to the end and be buried by the sons
stops.campa: Whether he is manumitted or simply stays on, the sources do not agree. Diogenes Laertius records that he grew old in the house of Xeniades and that the sons buried him. The family, asked afterward what sort of man they had bought, is supposed to have answered that a good spirit had come into the house. He keeps the Craneum through it all, and the jar, and the public life. No document of the purchase or the freeing survives; there is only the biography, written six hundred years later.
stops.quote: he grew old in the house of Xeniades, and when he died was buried by his sons.
suggested_refs: The house of Xeniades at Corinth, where the tradition has him spend his last years

stops.name: Corinth, the Peirene spring: the cup thrown away
stops.date_confidence: traditional; Diogenes Laertius gives no place for the scene, and the siting at Peirene comes from later tradition and from painters, not from the record
stops.campa: He is carrying a wooden cup in his wallet, the last object he owns past cloak, staff, and wallet. At the water he sees a child drinking out of its cupped hands. He takes the cup out and throws it away. The subtraction has been running for forty years, and this is where the record stops counting. Diogenes Laertius sets a second scene beside it in the same passage: a boy whose bowl had broken, eating his lentils out of a hollowed piece of bread. The bowl goes after the cup.
stops.quote: A child has beaten me in plainness of living.
suggested_refs: The Peirene fountain at Corinth, where later tradition and painting set the discarding of the cup

stops.name: Corinth, the books under his name
stops.date_confidence: the list of titles is transmitted by Diogenes Laertius; the authenticity of the works was already disputed in antiquity and nothing survives intact
stops.campa: A list of titles comes down under his name: dialogues, a set of tragedies, and a Republic describing a city with no currency, no weapons worth the name, no marriage, and men living as the animals live. Nothing of it survives whole. Some in antiquity held that the tragedies were written by his pupil Philiscus of Aegina and merely circulated as his; others struck the entire list out as forgery. Within a century of his death the man was carrying a shelf of books under his name. Whether he wrote any of them cannot now be decided.
suggested_refs: The catalogue of works attributed to Diogenes at Diogenes Laertius 6.80, including the lost Republic and the Pordalos

stops.name: Corinth, the Craneum: the death
stops.date_confidence: the year 323 BCE comes from the tradition synchronizing his death with Alexander's; Censorinus makes him 81 at death, another strand about 90, and the cause is disputed outright
stops.campa: He dies at Corinth, about ninety years old by one count and eighty-one by another. On the cause, Diogenes Laertius lays out the versions and adjudicates none of them: that he held his breath deliberately until it stopped; that he ate a raw octopus and was seized with colic; that a dog bit him in the foot while he was sharing out an octopus among dogs and the wound killed him; that it was a fever, or simply age. Demetrius of Magnesia adds that he died the same day as Alexander at Babylon, and reports it flatly.
stops.quote: He was seized with colic after eating an octopus raw and so met his end.
suggested_refs: Demetrius of Magnesia, On Men of the Same Name, source of the synchronism with Alexander's death

stops.name: Corinth, his instructions for the body
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the instruction is transmitted in more than one incompatible form
stops.campa: He leaves word that they are to throw him out unburied, or into a ditch, and let the animals have what is left. Another version has him ask to be thrown into the Ilissus so as to be of use to his brothers, which is a river at Athens and not at Corinth, and nobody has reconciled that. Asked whether it does not trouble him to be eaten by dogs, he is supposed to have said they should lay his stick beside him to drive them off; told that he would not be there to feel it, he asked then what harm the dogs could do him.
stops.quote: Some say that when dying he left instructions that they should throw him out unburied.
suggested_refs: The competing burial instructions preserved at Diogenes Laertius 6.79

stops.name: Corinth, the gate toward the Isthmus
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the grave has never been recovered by excavation, and Pausanias' description of the Craneion does not mention it
stops.campa: The Corinthians bury him anyway, with a public funeral, by the gate that leads out toward the Isthmus on the eastern side of the city. Over the grave they set up a pillar with a dog cut in Parian marble on top of it. The dispute over his body is settled the way the dispute over his coin was settled, by other people, in his absence, according to their own custom. Pausanias walked that road centuries later and wrote down the cypresses, the precinct of Bellerophon, and the tomb of Lais, without mentioning him.
suggested_refs: The pillar and Parian marble dog raised over the grave, reported at Diogenes Laertius 6.78
sources: Pausanias 2.2.4 (the Craneion, with no mention of the grave)

stops.name: Sinope, the bronze statues and the epigram
stops.date_confidence: traditional; Diogenes Laertius gives the epigram as an inscription and names no author for it
stops.campa: The city that lost him, or expelled him, sets up bronze statues of him carrying an inscription: time makes even bronze grow old, but your glory, Diogenes, all eternity will never destroy. Diogenes Laertius reports the lines without an author. By then the coinage scandal has become a story about a philosopher rather than a case of fraud, and the mint town has an asset in it. There is no record of what became of the statues. Sinope goes on striking silver through the Hellenistic centuries, eagle on dolphin, magistrate's name on the die.
suggested_refs: The bronze statues and inscribed epigram at Sinope, reported at Diogenes Laertius 6.78

stops.name: Fiume, the house of Diogenes
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: In the Adriatic city D'Annunzio has seized and is running as his own state, Guido Keller builds himself a tree-house, sleeps half undressed beside a trained eagle, walks the beach with nothing on, and calls the way he is living the house of Diogenes. He gives it that name himself; it is not a later reader's comparison. The jar, the nakedness, the animal, the refusal of the local money and manners are assembled deliberately, in a town that is at that moment printing its own currency and writing its own constitution. The eagle is called Guido, after him.
suggested_refs: Guido Keller's tree-house at Fiume, October 1920, named by him 'the house of Diogenes'

stops.name: Sinop, the statue on the waterfront
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Twenty-three centuries on, the Turkish town standing on the same isthmus puts up a new statue by the sculptor Turan Bas: Diogenes upright on a barrel, a lamp in his hand, a dog at his feet. The barrel is the Latin mistranslation of his jar, the lamp is the midday marketplace, the dog is the name he was called in the street. The isthmus is the same one, the double harbor still works, and the name of the town has only shortened. The city that expelled him for defacing its currency raised the monument on its waterfront in 2006.
